items.title: My body. My pregnancy. - Between anxiety and anticipation | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>Being pregnant is a profound experience. How does it affect the body and mind? What counts as a high-risk pregnancy? How does stress affect the baby? Anticipation and worry go hand in hand.

The film follows three women through their pregnancies. Young city-dweller Assia is expecting her first child. On the one hand, she is full of anticipation and optimism. At the same time, she struggles with the physical changes that come with pregnancy. Tamara is already a mother. She is expecting twins and her pregnancy is therefore considered to be high-risk. To avoid premature labor, she has to take it easy - a challenge for her. The documentary also follows the pregnant Kathy. After longing for a child for a long time, she suddenly became pregnant "just like that.” She faces many fears and worries until she finally holds her baby in her arms.

The documentary provides a scientifically grounded look at how closely mother and child are connected - and how a baby changes not only the body, but a person’s entire life.

items.title: How the Iran war accidentally boosted clean energy | The Gray Area
items.author: Vox
items.content:
<article>Could a war that disrupted the world’s oil supply end up accelerating the shift away from it?

Subscribe to our channel! http://goo.gl/0bsAjO

In today’s episode, Vox senior reporter and producer Miles Bryan talks with Jason Bordoff, founding director of Columbia University’s Center on Global Energy Policy and a former Obama energy adviser, about an unintended upside of the Iran war: the impact on global energy consumption. They explore why energy security can motivate change where climate warnings haven’t, how China is poised to take advantage of this moment, and whether the US risks getting left behind.
 
The war in Iran has given countries a powerful reason to embrace green energy: protecting themselves from the next oil shock. Solar panels, batteries, and electric vehicles aren’t just tools for fighting climate change. They’re increasingly a way to secure affordable energy in a world where a distant conflict can upend daily life. But the same search for cheap, reliable power is also driving investment in coal, oil, and gas, raising the question of how much this crisis will actually change.

items.title: How China’s Export Machine Is Beating Tariffs
items.author: Bloomberg Originals
items.content:
<article>Tariffs and trade barriers thrown up by the US and Europe were supposed to slow China’s export machine. Instead, it has accelerated. China’s trade surplus this year is on track to exceed the $1.2 trillion record set in 2025.

While China’s exports to the West dropped between 2024 and 2025, its exports to Southeast Asia, South and Central America, Africa, Japan and South Korea all increased. And it’s not only about finding new markets abroad: China also has moved up the value chain. The country is now a major force in everything from electric cars and solar panels to robots and artificial intelligence.

But China’s export boom is unfolding against a fragile domestic backdrop. The country continues to grapple with weak consumer demand, a prolonged property downturn and high youth unemployment, making exports an increasingly important source of growth.

items.title: Jellyfish - The ocean's new rulers? | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>Jellyfish have been around for more than 500 million years. They don't have a heart, a brain or a skeleton, and are 90 percent water. But the damage they're able to inflict often makes the headlines.

Despite an apparently basic physical makeup, they possess remarkable abilities. Some species are highly poisonous, whereas others are considered virtually immortal. Will jellyfish become the future rulers of the seas?

Their long evolutionary history means jellyfish are now present in all the world's oceans. But their growing prevalence poses challenges for both people and the natural world: They sting bathers, disrupt the cooling systems of power stations and threaten fisheries and aquaculture.

For decades now, jellyfish blooms in the Mediterranean, in the Norwegian fjords and off the coast of Namibia have been occurring with increasing frequency, altering marine ecosystems and displacing fish. These creatures benefit from characteristics that make them exceptional survivors.

They've outlived the dinosaurs. In our ever-changing marine environment, could jellyfish also emerge again as the great survivors?

The First Crusade was one of the most extraordinary, bloody and significant episodes in medieval history. It began with an appeal for aid from the Christian Byzantine Empire, threatened by the rising power of the Muslim Seljuk Turks. But when Pope Urban II preached his sermon at Clermont in 1095, the result was unlike anything the world had ever seen.

Hundreds of thousands answered the call — lords, knights, peasants and priests — driven by religious fervour, the promise of salvation, and the dream of liberating the most sacred city on earth: Jerusalem. What followed was a years-long ordeal across thousands of miles of brutal terrain, marked by battles, sieges, starvation and treachery.

Now fully remastered with all-new animation, this is the story of how a medieval army, on the brink of annihilation more than once, somehow achieved the impossible.

items.title: Mao & Madam Mao - Purging 50 Million People Documentary
items.author: The People Profiles
items.content:
<article>Chairman Mao and Madame Mao documentary: Mao Zedong and Jiang Qing, from the Long March to the Cultural Revolution and the fall of the Gang of Four.

On 1 October 1949 Mao Zedong stood on Tiananmen Gate in Beijing and proclaimed the People's Republic of China, beginning 27 years of rule over the world's most populous nation. Born into a peasant family in Shaoshan, Hunan, in 1893, he was a delegate at the Chinese Communist Party's first congress in Shanghai in 1921 and rose to lead the party during the Long March of 1934–35. In Yan'an in 1938 he married Jiang Qing, a former Shanghai actress known by the stage name Lan Ping. After the Great Leap Forward caused a famine that killed tens of millions, Mao launched the Cultural Revolution in 1966 with Jiang Qing as one of its driving forces. Less than a month after his death in September 1976 she was arrested with the rest of the Gang of Four, and their televised trial ended in a death sentence in 1981, later commuted to life imprisonment, before she took her own life in 1991.

items.title: Congo's blood minerals - The high price of high-tech | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>Without coltan, the digital world would grind to a halt. The coveted mineral is used in cellphones, computers and countless other high-tech products.

The consequences of the world's hunger for raw materials are particularly visible in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo. A significant share of the world's coltan is mined there. Consumers around the globe benefit from modern technology, with its supply chain that can often be traced back to the Kivu region and its mines. Armed groups there fight for control over the lucrative deposits. The men, women and children that mine the coveted ore often do so under threat, and in life-threatening conditions. Covert trading networks deliver coltan to the global market. This documentary follows the mineral's journey and exposes the mechanisms of a system in which natural-resource wealth, violence and economic interest are closely interwoven.

items.title: How US intervention is changing Venezuela
items.author: Vox
items.content:
<article>In the days after the military operation that ousted Nicolás Maduro, a poll from the Caracas‑based firm Meganálisis showed that 92% of Venezuelans were grateful to President Donald Trump for removing Maduro and that 90% wanted the US as Venezuela’s main ally. During the months since, the US has been heavily involved in shaping Venezuela’s future. But some key reforms are moving slower than Venezuelans hoped for. 

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has laid out a three-step plan for US intervention in Venezuela: stability, recovery, and a transition to democracy. While plans for political reforms and democratic elections in Venezuela are moving slowly, the designs for who controls its oil have been moving fast. The US recently announced an agreement with Venezuela as “the biggest oil deal in world history.” 

As Venezuelans hold out hope that the final step in Rubio’s plan, a transition to democracy, will still materialize, support among Venezuelans for Trump appears to be slipping. According to a new Meganálisis poll, 83% of Venezuelans don’t believe Trump wants what is best for their country. As voices grow louder from opposition leaders like Nobel Peace Prize winner María Corina Machado to jumpstart democratic processes, pressure on the US is mounting to make good on their promise. 

Hosted by Kahlil Greene, this video is part of our new series, Kahlil Explains, that unites Vox’s unique brand of explainer journalism with Greene’s expertise in how politics and culture shape society. This episode traces the events that led to Maduro’s ousting, the lingering discord between the Venezuelan government and its people, and how US intervention is shaping the country’s future.

More than 16 years after it was signed into law, the Affordable Care Act — also known as “Obamacare” — is still a flashpoint in American life and politics. “Obama’s Deal,” a FRONTLINE documentary that’s now available to stream on YouTube for the first time, tells the story of how this historic — and controversial — piece of legislation was passed. 

In the documentary, veteran FRONTLINE producer Michael Kirk and his team took viewers behind the headlines and revealed the political maneuvering behind the healthcare reform bill’s passage, along party lines, in March 2010.

The passage followed a bruising year of debate, negotiation and backlash. Through interviews with administration officials, senators and Washington lobbyists, “Obama’s Deal” traced the dramatic details of how an idealistic president pursued the health care fight — despite the warnings of many of his closest advisers — and how he ended up making deals with many of the powerful special interests he had campaigned against.

“Obama’s Deal” was a FRONTLINE co-production with Kirk Documentary Group, Ltd. It was written and directed by Michael Kirk. It was produced by Michael Kirk, Jim Gilmore and Mike Wiser. It was reported by Jim Gilmore. The executive producer of FRONTLINE was David Fanning.

items.title: Nature and risk for likes - How social media is changing extreme sports | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>Extreme sports like cliff diving and mountaineering set against spectacular natural landscapes attract millions of views on social media. But what happens when taking risks becomes content?

Professional alpinist and mountain guide Michi Wohlleben and influencer Pauli Vogler approach the mountains from very different perspectives. For Michi, it’s all about skill, experience and being prepared for the challenges of the mountains. For Pauli, it’s all about content. She documents her trips with her smartphone and collaborates with brands.
Images of alpine adventures are inspiring and entertaining. But there is growing criticism of the role of social media in extreme sports. Pauli also faces backlash, despite making a conscious effort to promote safety, training and responsibility.

This dynamic is particularly evident in cliff jumping. Cliff diving and death diving are spectacular disciplines that synergize well with social media. The international community is closely connected and reaches a huge audience. But the limits of what is possible are constantly being pushed further and further.

Hans Preissler was seriously injured while jumping from a 30-meter-high cliff. Footage of his accident was viewed millions of times but also attracted abusive comments. 
Three years later, he is returning to the cliff. Will he jump again?

This documentary explores how social media is changing the way we view extreme sports, and how the fascination they exert is increasingly intertwined with self-promotion and image-making, community, commercial interests and risk.

ABSTRACT
"It doesn't matter: The only thing that'll read this code is another AI."

I hear people say it all the time. And they might be correct that their code will only ever be consumed by Claude or Codex. But that definitely doesn't mean the code's quality is irrelevant. Just about every good practice we've settled on over the last 50 years still applies when machines write our code. In fact, I believe that many of these principles are even more important, because (not surprisingly) AIs are making the same mistakes we make. They're just doing it faster.

Let me show you some ways to hold your AI coding buddy to a higher standard.

items.title: Why a “stable” labor market feels so bad | Best of Luck with Kyla Scanlon
items.author: Vox
items.content:
<article>Is it you, or is it the economy? 

You’ve sent the applications. You’ve done the coffee chats. Nothing. At some point you start to wonder what’s broken: you, or the job market?

There is arguably no one better equipped to answer this question than Claudia Sahm. Claudia invented what’s known as the “Sahm Rule,” one of the most respected rules in macroeconomics. You can think of it like a smoke detector for the economy. It beeps in warning when certain conditions are met. 

In this episode: Claudia explains why it feels so hard to find a job right now, why a “stable” labor market is not necessarily a good one, and what you can do about it. Plus: how she navigated the lowest points of her career (even legendary economists have to job hunt).

<article>The aircraft carrier USS Theodore Roosevelt has arrived in the Middle East to help the U.S. fend off Iranian attacks in the Strait of Hormuz, enforce the blockade and give President Trump expanded options to strike Iran should he choose to do so. The warship joins USS George Washington and USS George H.W. Bush, marking the second time this year that the U.S. has had three carriers in the Middle East. 

The U.S. has kept at least two carriers in the region since the war started, and so far five of the Navy’s 11 aircraft carriers have deployed to support the war. Two of those carriers, USS Gerald R. Ford and USS Abraham Lincoln, have set modern-day records for their length of deployment and their time at sea without a port call. The deployment of USS George H.W. Bush, which is in the Arabian Sea, has also been extended.

WSJ journalists visited USS George Washington in the Arabian Sea in October to learn more about how these carriers are conducting operations, and how the war is testing the limits of the Navy’s carrier strike groups. ABSTRACT
In 2026, "Engineering for Reality" means acknowledging that software ownership is a human challenge as much as a technical one. The mantra "you ship it, you own it" only works if engineers have the confidence to face production without fear. Confidence isn't a personality trait—it is an engineered outcome of focused training.

When engineers are left to "sink or swim", it breeds stress, imposter syndrome, and attrition. To enable them to build and operate software with confidence, we must build their confidence through targeted and reliable learning programs underpinned by Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) principles and best practices.

Drawing on proven methodologies from Google’s SRE EDU program, this session provides a blueprint for transforming training from a passive lecture into a reliability-critical asset, one where learning drives confidence, confidence drives behavior, and that behavior repeated over time enables a “you build it, you ship it, you own it” culture.)

items.title: Living with grief - How to cope with loss | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>The death of a loved one throws many people off course. This is certainly the case for Anja, who suffers greatly when her mother passes. The experience leaves her wondering what can help support the grieving, as well as how societies process grief.

Anja's mother dies suddenly. The two were very close; her mother was like a best friend. And she was still very young, just 55 years old. Anja wasn't in any way prepared for the sense of loss that followed. "I thought I'd never be able to laugh again," she says. Grief calls everything into question: Priorities, relationships, one's outlook on life itself. Nothing feels the same as it did before - including Anja herself, who realizes she's also changed. She wonders why she was so unprepared. What place does grief have in our society, and what can really help those left behind when a loved one dies? Anja sets out in search of answers.
She meets people experiencing grief in very different ways. She talks to Benedictine monk Anselm Grün about the importance of rituals as a source of comfort in times of loss. She also experiences Dia de los Muertos in Berlin, a Latin American custom that celebrates grief in a very visible and vibrant way. Even within her own family, grief looks very different. Anja's father has his own way of dealing with the death of his wife.
Years pass before Anja and her father find closeness once again - a narrative that runs through the documentary. Anja Umland also decides to involve her children in the grieving process. While some say "Don't cry in front of the kids...", she's honest and open with them about her feelings. Today, grief hasn't gone away, but has found a permanent place in her life. She keeps her mother's memory alive with small personal rituals. Life has changed, but now grief, love and life are allowed to coexist within it.

For nearly six weeks, he survived alone inside an abandoned Fairbanks 142 bus, more than 20 miles from the nearest road... but the wilderness was about to test everything he believed about survival.

LAST DAYS is Weird History’s prestige format series focusing on final chapters, deaths, downfalls and conclusions. In this episode, we examine what happened during McCandless’s final days to figure out how a young man seeking absolute freedom became trapped in the wild and what mistakes ultimately led to the tragic ending of his journey.

items.title: Racism in the church - People of Color battle for representation | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>Racism has many faces, even within the Christian faith. Those affected cite workplace discrimination; People of Color are underrepresented in senior positions. Can prejudice be overcome?

For a long time, Christian church campaigns mostly portrayed people from the Global South as people in need of aid. That's set to change: People of Color are calling for a greater say and stronger representation on church bodies. The church is responding - yet racist attitudes and hostility persist.

For pastor Égide Muziazia, discriminatory insults forced him out of public life - but also fostered greater solidarity within the Catholic Diocese of Münster.

Sarah Vecera works for an international communion of Protestant churches. She writes, hosts her own podcast and runs anti-racism workshops. Nicolas Moumouni is an advisor on intercultural development for the Evangelical Lutheran Church in Northern Germany, and Father Uchenna Aba from Goch-Kessel in North Rhine-Westphalia draws upon his African heritage in his work as a Catholic chaplain.

items.title: Luxury living and the ultra-rich - When money is no object | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>Sell a penthouse for 12 million euros? Build a luxury villa with an infinity pool? Just another average working day in the lives of Mira van der Zalm and Jürgen Willen: They design and sell luxury properties.

Discretion is paramount here. "German clients tend to be rather reserved when it comes to luxury, whereas foreign clients like to show off what they have," says Jürgen Willen - and he knows what he's talking about. On almost every continent, the architect and his team design luxury villas and interiors for a clientele seeking something truly unique. From bathtubs to car lifts with washing facilities, if it's on the wish-list and can be done, Willen will make it happen.
Mira van der Zalm's client base is equally discerning. The estate agent arranges the sale of houses and flats not advertised on the open market - that takes a special level of service. For example, she calls in Jürgen Willen to an Art Nouveau villa in Wiesbaden to check whether it's possible to install an underground parking lot and a spa - and if it can be done in accordance with listed building regulations.

items.title: Our parents are scrolling their lives away | The Gray Area
items.author: Vox
items.content:
<article>When your aging parents can’t put down their phones, where does care end and control begin?

Subscribe to our channel! http://goo.gl/0bsAjO

In this episode, Vox reporter and producer Miles Bryan talks with internet culture reporter Jessica Lucas about the older adults who are getting hooked on AI-generated videos, and their grown children who are trying to intervene. Her reporting follows families navigating sleepless nights, health misinformation, subscription traps, and an uncomfortable reversal: the parents who may have once warned their kids about screen time as children, now need help managing their own.

They explore how grief and loneliness can draw people into endless scrolling, who profits from keeping them there, and what researchers can (and can’t) tell us about the effects on the aging brain. They also consider the ethical questions facing families who secretly change passwords, curate feeds, or install restrictions. How do you protect someone without taking away their independence, or the online connections that still bring them joy?

items.title: How To Take a Picture of a Black Hole | PODCAST: The Joy of Why
items.author: Quanta Magazine
items.content:
<article>Astrophysicist Shep Doeleman explains how capturing the first image of a black hole required a telescope the size of the world, and why the next goal is to create a movie.

“The Joy of Why” is a Quanta Magazine podcast about curiosity and the pursuit of knowledge. The mathematician and author Steven Strogatz and the cosmologist and author Janna Levin take turns interviewing leading researchers about the great scientific and mathematical questions of our time.  For more episodes visit Quanta Magazine: https://www.quantamagazine.org/tag/the-joy-of-why/

--------

00:00 Why black holes fascinate us
03:27 Meet Shep Doeleman
06:44 How we knew black holes existed
11:28 Turning Earth into a telescope
19:24 Building the Event Horizon Telescope
26:19 M87 vs. Sagittarius A*
35:06 Revealing the first black hole image
39:10 Why black holes look like rings
42:55 Making movies of black holes
46:25 What black hole movies could reveal
49:28 Testing alternatives to black holes
53:12 The joy of seeing the invisible

---------

Black holes are one of the universe’s most exotic and elusive objects. When nothing, not even light, can escape their powerful gravitational grasp, taking a picture of one seems unimaginable. But an image of a black hole, or more accurately its shadow, could offer insights that theory alone may not provide when testing predictions. So how can it be done?

Harvard astrophysicist Shep Doeleman and a team of 250 researchers achieved this extraordinary feat by linking a group of radio telescopes around the world. This network, called the Event Horizon Telescope, produced the first image of a supermassive black hole in the galaxy M87, around 55 million light-years away, and the first image of the black hole at the heart of our galaxy. In this episode, Doeleman tells co-host Janna Levin how he turned the Earth into a telescope capable of seeing a black hole, the incredible level of science and collaboration that was required to achieve this, how the images have furthered our understanding of these exotic objects, and how movies of black holes may be possible by the early 2030s.

items.title: Creatine, debunked
items.author: Vox
items.content:
<article>Creatine is everywhere right now. But are the claims around this classic supplement actually based in real science? Or are they just more marketing hype?

For decades, creatine has been sold to fitness buffs, as a way to build more muscle, faster. Now it’s being pitched to almost everyone, with influencers, podcasters and celebrity doctors claiming it can sharpen your mind, lift your mood, offset sleep deprivation, and even reverse the effects of Alzheimer’s disease. And these wellness claims are driving a real surge in profit — US sales topped half a billion dollars in 2025. 

So what is creatine actually doing in your body? Will it really help you build muscle, or are those dramatic before-and-after photos telling a different story? And when it comes to your brain, is there real evidence behind the claims about memory, mood, and Alzheimer’s, or is the hype getting ahead of the science?

We dug into the research on creatine, from the muscles to the mind, and spoke with exercise scientist Nick Tiller and associate professor Matthew Taylor, whose team at the University of Kansas studied creatine’s effects on people with Alzheimer’s disease.

Read more about the real science behind creatine:

But what is the stock market actually like in this day and age? Is there a bustling trading floor, with investors shouting "Buy!" and "Sell"?

Today's stock market is quite different. After a stock market shake-up known as the Big Bang in 1986, the bustling trading floor was replaced with people making trades by phone from their own offices. Nowadays, trading activity takes place on computer servers. Traders and investors can do it all from investing apps on their phones.

It's still fascinating to be able to see inside the real stock market. I'm using this as an opportunity to explain how the stock market actually works. I'll take you through the history of the stock market, what "shares" actually are, what actually happens when you buy stocks on the stock market, all the different kinds of investments you can buy on the stock market such as ETFs, Options and Futures, and everything else you need to know as a modern investor. 

If you're look to build wealth and achieve financial freedom through investing, this overview of the stock market and how the stock market works will be an essential video for you!

items.title: The unicorn - In pursuit of magic | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>For centuries, the unicorn has roamed through cultural history, myths and fairy tales. It's been a symbol of healing, destruction - even queer identity. How has this fantastical creature so captured our imaginations?

Legend has it that ever since ancient times, the unicorn has lived in hiding. If it reveals itself at all, it's only ever for a moment - and only ever from a distance. One of the world's most famous mythical creatures, it's been galloping across our cultural histories for centuries. It appears in works of art, on coats of arms and altars, at fountains, on buildings and everyday objects. It appears in fantasy films, has become a symbol of queer identity and an icon of pop culture.

The myth of the unicorn can be traced back to the second millennium B.C. Only quite late in history did it become clear the creature existed in fact only in our imaginations - and yet our fascination with it has never died.

Over time, it's been attributed with countless meanings. It's been thought of as both healing and destructive, wild and untamable, while still serving as a symbol of purity and innocence. And it has always been associated with a deep longing - after someone caught a glimpse of one, they could supposedly never forget it.

But - has anyone ever really seen a unicorn? Where did the idea of a horse with a horn growing from its forehead first come from? How has an animal that has never existed been able to awaken such powerful, true yearning in us for thousands of years? The hunt for its tracks is on...

ABSTRACT
In Helsinki, there is a public playground where children learn how computers work. A six-metre tower you climb into as a data packet and slide out as output. A flowchart hopscotch where you jump through conditional statements. A binary abacus you move with your whole body.

Linda Liukas designed this playground. Some computational ideas translated into physical space beautifully. Others fell apart the moment they had to survive a four-year-old. This is a talk about the distance between an abstraction and a body, and the oldest question in computing: how do you make something complex feel simple, without making it simple?

items.title: Why are fewer Black Americans getting GLP-1s?
items.author: Vox
items.content:
<article>GLP-1s have become the newest celebrity miracle drug, with famous athletes like Serena Williams and Charles Barkley sharing that they’ve used it for weight loss.

Drugs like Ozempic and Wegovy have become a status symbol. But before they were famous, GLP-1s were developed to treat Type 2 diabetes, a disease that occurs when a person’s blood sugar becomes too high. It affects nearly 40 million Americans and hits Black Americans especially hard. According to the CDC, about 12 percent of Black adults have diabetes, compared with roughly 7 percent of white adults. Yet when researchers reviewed 26 studies from across the country, they found that Black patients were about 20 percent less likely than white patients to be prescribed newer diabetes drugs.

That gap has deep roots. A century ago, doctors called diabetes a “luxury disease” of wealthy white and Jewish people, and many didn’t believe Black people could get the disease at all. Even after the landmark 1985 Heckler Report exposed stark racial disparities in American health, Black patients’ diabetes was often blamed on lifestyle rather than on the housing, food, financial, and healthcare inequities shaping their health.

Hosted by Kahlil Greene, this video is part of our series, Kahlil Explains, which unites Vox’s unique brand of explainer journalism with Greene’s expertise in how politics and culture shape society. This episode traces the history of race and diabetes in America to unpack why Black patients are still less likely to get access to GLP-1s, and why closing that gap will take more than a prescription.

Read more about GLP-1s, diabetes, and race in American medicine:

- Arleen Tuchman’s book Diabetes: A History of Race and Disease: https://www.jstor.org/stable/j.ctv14rmqdm

- JAMA Health Forum’s study on racial and income disparities in GLP-1 prescriptions: https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama-health-forum/fullarticle/2787276

- The Journal of General Internal Medicine’s review of racial disparities in diabetes drug access: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11606-026-10178-z

- University of Colorado Anschutz’s explainer on how GLP-1 drugs went from lab discovery to weight-loss breakthrough: https://news.cuanschutz.edu/news-stories/how-glp-1-drugs-went-from-lab-discovery-to-weight-loss-breakthroughs

- Tablet magazine’s article on Diabetes, the Jewish disease: https://www.tabletmag.com/sections/science/articles/diabetes-jewish-disease-tuchman

- The original 1985 Heckler Report on Black and minority health: https://collections.nlm.nih.gov/ext/heckler/8602912X1/PDF/8602912X1.pdf

items.title: Inside Appalachia’s Black Lung Crisis | Coal’s Human Cost (full documentary) | FRONTLINE (PBS)
items.author: FRONTLINE PBS | Official
items.content:
<article>An investigation into the resurgence of black lung disease among veteran Appalachian coal miners & the failures to protect them. 

This journalism is made possible by viewers like you. Donate to FRONTLINE now: https://bit.ly/47DFzCb

And support your local PBS station here: https://www.pbs.org/donate

Working veteran underground coal miners in central Appalachia are suffering from black lung disease at the highest rates in nearly 50 years. It’s now as bad as the 1970s, with thousands of miners sick and dying. Meanwhile, the Trump administration has been boosting coal mining, with a pledge of nearly $700 million to keep coal-fired power plants running and coal exports flowing.

“Coal’s Human Cost,” an investigative documentary eight years in the making from FRONTLINE, NPR, Public Health Watch and the Appalachia + Mid-South Newsroom tracks the resurgence of this disease in Appalachia, its impact on miners and their families, and the role of the government and the mining industry in failing to protect them. 

The documentary also examines how doctors and advocates have been trying for years to sound the alarm and to get better protections for miners.

“This has been going on for decades,” says Drew Harris, a pulmonologist and medical director at black lung clinics who has worked with hundreds of sick miners over the years “And we know why this is happening, and it is entirely preventable, and we aren’t preventing it.” 

“Coal’s Human Cost” is a FRONTLINE production with Five O’Clock Films in association with Forage Media. The writer, producer and director is Molly Born. The producer and correspondent is Howard Berkes. The senior producer is Frank Koughan. The managing editor of FRONTLINE is Andrew Metz. items.title: Living with dwarfism and fighting prejudice | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>This documentary follows three people with dwarfism as they fight for greater inclusion. An activist, a politician, and an actor are seeking to combat prejudice and improve their visibility in society.

In Spain, Yesica Expósito Alvarez has spearheaded legislation that prevents people with disabilities from being exploited for entertainment. "Comic” bullfights, for example, featuring people with dwarfism dressed in costumes, were a longstanding Spanish tradition until new legislation came into force. Today, she’s fighting for healthcare tailored to the needs of people with dwarfism. If doctors conducting emergency surgery, for example, are unaware of certain differences, it can be fatal for the patient.
Simone Fischer is the first woman with dwarfism to serve as a member of the German parliament. She advocates for a society that excludes no one. As a child, she lacked role models. Now, she’s committed to encouraging young women in particular to take on political responsibility.
Mick Morris Mehnert is an actor in Germany who advocates for a nuanced portrayal of people with disabilities in film and theater. Although Mehnert has taken on some roles in fairytale films, he doesn’t want to be stereotyped. To raise awareness, he’s producing his own web series together with his father and friends.

items.title: How an Effort to Shield Coal Miners From Black Lung Fell Apart | FRONTLINE @NPR @pubhealthwatch
items.author: FRONTLINE PBS | Official
items.content:
<article>Watch a video drawn from "Coal's Human Cost," a Nov. 2026 investigative documentary from @frontline, @NPR, @pubhealthwatch & the Appalachia + Mid-South Newsroom.  

This journalism is made possible by viewers like you. Donate to FRONTLINE now: https://bit.ly/47DFzCb

And support your local PBS station here: https://www.pbs.org/donate

When Johnathan Wright began working underground in coal mines more than 25 years ago, the percentage of veteran working coal miners in Central Appalachia diagnosed with black lung disease was down to roughly one in 10. 

Today, that reported rate is the highest it’s been since 1978: One in three — and Wright, age 44, has joined them.

“It’s awful,” says Wright, who was diagnosed with the incurable disease in 2023 after he started struggling to breathe when climbing the Kentucky hills, and began coughing up grey phlegm. “You work your whole life to enjoy the rest of it, and then you can't enjoy it.”

Wright is among the coal miners who share their stories in Coal’s Human Cost, a new documentary from FRONTLINE, NPR, Public Health Watch and the Appalachia + Mid-South Newsroom. Its Nov. 10, 2026, premiere comes as the Trump administration has been boosting coal mining, including through a pledge of nearly $700 million to keep coal-fired power plants running and coal exports flowing.

Against that backdrop, "Coal’s Human Cost" tracks the resurgence of black lung disease in Appalachia, the impact on miners and their families, and the role of the government and the mining industry in failing to protect them. 

“It just still amazes me after all these years that these conditions have not been improved," Ron Carson, a retired director of black lung clinics, tells correspondent Howard Berkes in the above video drawn from the documentary.

items.title: How NIL Deals Are Turning High-School Sports Into Big Business | WSJ
items.author: The Wall Street Journal
items.content:
<article>Amateur athletes’ ability to sign endorsement deals that monetize their name, image, and likeness has pumped billions of dollars into college sports. Now it’s coming for high school athletes. 

For some parents and coaches, NIL deals create welcome opportunities for students to offset the growing costs of elite youth sports. items.title: Chocolate is getting worse. So is everything else. | The Gray Area
items.author: Vox
items.content:
<article>If even chocolate is getting worse, what does that tell us about our economy and the state of life’s small pleasures?

Subscribe to our channel! http://goo.gl/0bsAjO

In today’s episode, Vox host Jonquilyn Hill talks to New York Magazine writer Rachel Handler, who spent seven months investigating that question and uncovered a story that goes well beyond candy. Handler explains how manufacturing has changed, what chocolate reveals about corporate profits and inequality, and why even life’s smallest pleasures increasingly feel like luxuries. 

They explore the hidden costs of convenience, whether we’ve learned to like inferior products, and the indignity of being told nothing has changed, even when we can taste the difference. What do we lose when we stop expecting everyday things to be good? And what would it take to make a decent chocolate bar an ordinary pleasure everyone can afford?

items.title: The Forgotten Way French Chefs Made Soup with Béchamel
items.author: French Cooking Academy
items.content:
<article>Did you know Auguste Escoffier used béchamel for a specific category of French soups called the creme (cream soups)? in this video I will take you through the process on how to make these forgotten type of soup that yields a rich, velvety recipe taken straight from the classic guide culinairre from Escoffier .

GET THE RECIPE: https://www.thefrenchcookingacademy.com/recipes/escoffier-cream-soup

SIGNUP TO MY FREE ONION SOUP COURSE: https://www.thefrenchcookingacademy.com/pot-au-feu-to-onion-soup

 In this video, you'll learn:
• How to build a clean, pale roux without burning it
• The right way to thin béchamel with stock for a soup consistency
• Escoffier's traditional liaison technique for a silky finish

⏱️ CHAPTERS:
0:00 - Escoffier’s Secret Soup Base
0:45 - Making the Perfect White Roux
2:15 - Infusing the Stock & Milk
4:30 - Simmering to the Right Thickness
6:10 - The Classic Liaison (Cream & Butter)
7:45 - Garnishing & Taste Test

INGREDIENTS:
Base bechamel
12.5 g Unsalted butter
12.5 g All-purpose flour
600 ml  Whole milk, warm
aromatics tbsp each( onion, carrot, celery, leek)
 thyme, bay leaf. 2 cloves
salt and peper

For the bean (soaked overnight and cooked after for 1 hour)
250 gram dry white bean
1 Bouquet garni (fresh thyme, bay leaf, parsley stems)
1 Small onion or white leek, finely sliced
1 carrot sliced
Sea salt & ground white pepper, to taste
3 cloves

Finishing:
• 100 ml bean cooking juices 
• 150 ml cream
• Croutons or fresh chervil/parsley for garnish

COOKING TIP:
• Always use white pepper instead of black pepper to keep the soup’s color clean.

items.title: The smoothest reorg": lessons in collaborative org design • Joakim Sundén • GOTO Copenhagen 2026
items.author: GOTO Conferences
items.content:
<article>This presentation was recorded at GOTO Copenhagen 2026. #GOTOcon #GOTOcph
Join us at GOTO Copenhagen 2027, October 4–8. https://gotocph.com/2027?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=video&utm_campaign=cph26-talks

Joakim Sundén - Founding partner at Better Product Work and co-creator of the Spotify model @joakimsunden3557 


RESOURCES
https://x.com/joakimsunden
https://www.linkedin.com/in/joakimsunden
https://joakimsunden.com/
https://bsky.app/profile/joakimsunden.bsky.social
https://gotopia.tech/experts/1286/joakim-sunden


ABSTRACT
Most reorgs create confusion and friction. Spotify developed a more collaborative way of approaching org design, where teams help shape their missions, boundaries and structure.

This talk is a career experience report about taking the lessons from that work and applying a similar approach, which we now call Collaborative Org Design, years later at a fast-growing B2B scale-up facing a shift in strategy and team topology.

Joakim will share what worked, what didn’t, how his team used ideas from Team Topologies and self-selection, and how initial skepticism turned into comments like “this was the smoothest reorg I’ve ever seen.”

You’ll leave with practical patterns, pitfalls and facilitation tips for involving teams directly in org design.

items.title: Stronger than the regime - Bodybuilders in East Germany | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>Bodybuilders were viewed with great suspicion by the government in the GDR. The Stasi kept many of them under surveillance. But these weightlifters weren't going to let that stop them - quite the opposite...

They made their own dumbbells and trained in attics, cellars or wherever they could find some space. The film tells the story of athletes who were masters of improvisation. "There were no gyms," says sports historian Dr Andreas Müller. Even the term 'bodybuilding' was officially taboo. "In the GDR, it was called 'physical culture'."

The athletes converted barracks into training rooms, swapped records for weights and bars, and smuggled specialist magazines in from the West to get hold of training programs. They also showed great creativity when it came to obtaining performance-enhancing drugs.

Who were these people? A question even the East German intelligence agency, known as the Stasi, couldn't answer in sufficient detail. Undercover agents signed up at sports clubs and trained alongside members; telephone calls were tapped and flats were bugged. 

Weightlifting developed in the shadow of state-organized competitive sport. Competitions in the West were banned, and even tournaments in the eastern bloc were often off-limits to GDR athletes. But still, the bodybuilders managed to evade state control. 

The Stasi grew increasingly exasperated. When the athletes tested the regime by flooding it with emigration applications, even unofficial informants leapt to their defense, claiming that the weightlifters were being treated unfairly, says historian Andreas Müller. Ironically, the informers eventually became advocates. To prevent high-profile defections and preserve its international sporting image, the GDR regime capitulated by granting the weightlifters prestigious "Master of Sport" awards.

items.title: Bangladesh and the climate crisis - Fleeing the floods | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>In southern Bangladesh, Lokkhi and her family prepare to move to Dhaka. They're escaping extreme climate change by going to one of the world's fastest growing cities.

With its flat, low-lying geography and large river deltas, exposed to rising sea levels, cyclones and storm surges, Bangladesh is one of the countries most vulnerable to climate change. The government predicts more extreme monsoons, tropical cyclones, heavy rain, and flooding.
With the threat of natural disaster hanging over their heads, Lokkhi and her family are preparing to leave their home before everything is washed away. Lokkhi is migrating to Dhaka - and she is not the only one. Every day, thousands of climate refugees arrive in the capital, one of the fastest growing cities in the world. How much longer will Dhaka be able to absorb so many people?

It's estimated that by 2050, nearly 20 percent of the southern coastline will be uninhabitable, and 30 million people will be displaced. The largest mass migration in human history is no longer a distant prospect; it's an inevitable reality. Bangladeshis are fighting for climate justice and compensation before it's too late. A bleak future that's already grim reality here in Bangladesh.

items.title: Code Health Guardian • Artie Shevchenko & Titus Winters • GOTO 2026
items.author: GOTO Conferences
items.content:
<article>This interview was recorded for the GOTO Book Club. #GOTOcon #GOTObookclub
http://gotopia.tech/bookclub

Check out more here:
https://gotopia.tech/episodes/460

Artie Shevchenko - Software Engineer at Canva & Author of "Code Health Guardian" @artie_shevchenko 
Titus Winters - Senior Principal Scientist at Adobe & Co-Curator of "Software Engineering at Google" @tituscsucredu 

RESOURCES
Artie
https://github.com/artie-shevchenko
https://www.linkedin.com/in/artie-shevchenko-67845a4b

Titus
https://x.com/TitusWinters
https://github.com/tituswinters
https://www.linkedin.com/in/tituswinters

Links
https://youtu.be/NNMnbBf0Itw
https://youtu.be/W7XL_LZgvKI
https://youtu.be/gAQ6t3F_2Ug

DESCRIPTION
Artie Shevchenko, a former Google engineer who is now at Canva and teaches at ITMO University, tells Titus Winters how his book “Code Health Guardian” came together: the internal code review classes he built at Google (over 1,000 Googlers attended, with a 4.5-star rating), a talk on A Philosophy of Software Design, and years of teaching a university course. He keeps that book's three complexity problems (change amplification, cognitive load, and unknown unknowns), which he says help you rank what to fix first. But he doesn't agree with its two causes, obscurity and dependencies. Dependencies are also the building blocks of all software, so he replaces them with six more specific causes: untrue interfaces, complex interfaces, unfamiliarity, too many dependencies, duplication, and unstable dependencies. Titus agrees that "all dependencies are bad" misses the point, since every dependency is both a benefit and a liability.

The AI conversation turns on understanding. Artie compares models to two types of exam students who give nearly identical answers: one who understands the material and one who memorized it. Most of the time you can get away with the second kind, but not always, so a human "code health guardian" still has to validate AI output or risk losing intellectual control of the codebase. He admits he's still learning how to prioritize reviews, and no longer reads every test line as carefully. Titus adds that his top worry is whatever is hardest to change later (dependencies, frameworks, state storage, API design, database schemas), which lines up with Artie's view that interfaces sit at the top of the list. They also discuss intellectual versus statistical control (tests as evidence), and Artie makes the case for "semi-functional programming," meaning immutability by default, which reduces obscurity. Titus ties it to testing: stateless code is trivial to test, and mutable state is where time enters the problem. Both stress that nobody has the full playbook for AI-assisted development yet.

TIMECODES
00:00 Intro
00:26 1,000 Googlers & a 4.5-star code review class
05:08 The 3 code complexity problems
10:50 Why we still need a human in the loop

Last week, hackers drained $6.3 billion from Binance, the world’s largest crypto exchange, in what blockchain analysts call the largest theft of any kind in history. items.title: From hate to peace - The power of reconciliation | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>Against hate and exclusion; for respect and tolerance. Initiatives in Germany, the U.S. and Colombia show how reconciliation can work - between religions, political opponents, victims and perpetrators.

Colombian Kelly Diaz was just a child when terrorists shot and killed her father. Now, 22 years on, she's meeting his killer in prison. She wants to forgive him and finally make peace with it all. For years now, a unique reconciliation project has been helping her prepare for that moment. It's an initiative launched by Stuttgart-based social entrepreneur Tobias Merckle. "It's a liberating process for both sides. Victims can leave hatred and thoughts of revenge behind, while perpetrators can take responsibility for their crimes and experience forgiveness," he says. Their journey doesn't end there, though. Both victims and perpetrators will go on to work together rebuilding places destroyed by civil war - what are known as "villages of reconciliation." 

Concern is also mounting over increasing political polarization in the United States. Republicans versus Democrats, right against left - the rifts in society seem to be deepening. The Braver Angels initiative is using dialogue as an attempt to turn that trend around. Since 2016, it's been running workshops where participants practice active listening and respectful debate. The goal is constructive exchange across the political divide.
Munich-based YouthBridge has made it its mission to prevent polarization from ever taking hold in the first place. It brings together young people from various backgrounds, from many religions and different walks of life. Jewish and Muslim college students engage in dialogue, alongside other young people from other cultural backgrounds. Can bridges be built to connect different communities? Is hate and exclusion preventable? "Our society is very divided, everyone retreats into their own bubble," says 18-year-old Begüm Tan. "We need to reach out again to one another, even if we don't always agree." YouthBridge trains young people to become multipliers who can develop their own social, cultural and media projects - promoting peaceful coexistence.

items.title: Sir John Hawkwood - Europe's Richest Mercenary Documentary
items.author: The People Profiles
items.content:
<article>Sir John Hawkwood: a documentary on the Essex-born captain of the White Company, the English condottiere who fought for Milan, the Pope and Florence.

Painted by Paolo Uccello on the wall of Florence Cathedral in 1436, Giovanni Acuto was in fact John Hawkwood, a tanner's son from Essex. After serving as a longbowman in the Hundred Years' War, he crossed into Italy with the White Company in 1361 and spent three decades selling his sword to Pisa, Milan, the Papacy, Padua and Florence. The story takes in the Cesena massacre, his marriage to Donnina Visconti, daughter of Bernabò Visconti, his victory at Castagnaro in 1387 and his death in Florence in 1394.

items.title: North Korea - Propaganda and the next generation | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>North Korea: A small country often at the center of global attention for geopolitical reasons. The Kim dynasty has ruled through oppression and isolation since 1948. Yet the regime is striving to project a new image.

Luxury resorts, an international marathon in the capital and a ruling family portrayed in a surprisingly approachable light: Recently, North Korea has been showing the world a very different face. Is the country, up until now known primarily for repression and isolation, undergoing an image change? This documentary looks behind the scenes and reveals the contradictions of a country caught between cautious openness and unrelenting control.

On one hand, a new apparent openness is emerging through sporting events attended by carefully selected international participants. Images of what looks like a thriving economy are being disseminated beyond the country's borders: Online shopping in Pyongyang, idyllic beaches with modern holiday facilities, and even streaming services for wealthy North Koreans loyal to the regime.

State television shows cheerful locals treating themselves to a break at the seaside resort of Wonsan after toiling hard for the motherland. Around 80 per cent of the population are now said to own a mobile phone - albeit with access restricted to state-approved North Korean apps.

Ruler Kim Jong Un is also embracing the image campaign, with more frequent public appearances alongside his daughter Kim Ju Ae. Is she being groomed to be a potential successor? Or is this family-centered turn intended to give the regime a more human face?

At the same time, the state continues to crack down hard on any form of undesirable behavior. Archival footage and reports from refugee organizations document public trials of young people caught consuming South Korean pop culture. International experts emphasize that a change in the country's public image by no means signifies an end to surveillance, punishment and censorship.

ABSTRACT
Have you seen early productivity gains from AI, only to watch them disappear under growing complexity and production incidents? You're not alone. There's a common reason: many production systems already struggle with technical debt. When AI agents enter the development loop, that debt becomes a multiplier. Poor-quality code not only increases defects and costs. It dramatically raises AI risk by driving high breakage rates, turning promising AI agents into legacy code generators rather than genuine help.

Fortunately, there's hope on the horizon. In this talk, Adam Tornhill shows how organizations can achieve both speed and quality with AI. Backed by large-scale empirical studies on AI coding and developer productivity, we separate what works from what doesn't in real-world systems. Building on these findings, we then look at a practical framework for driving and sustaining AI-friendly code at scale. The AI revolution is here. Is your code ready?

items.title: Why the right can't stop talking about communism
items.author: Vox
items.content:
<article>There’s been a lot of “communist” talk on the midterms campaign trail. It’s become Trump’s favorite new perceived threat coming from the left. But it’s actually not new at all. 

US politicians, especially on the right, have long described communism as a threat to the American way of life. As a result, the United States has undergone historical periods of intense and occasionally violent means to suppress the spread of communism. Beyond the clash between capitalism and communism as economic systems, a line is often drawn between communist ideology and religion in America, specifically Christianity. 

In the 1950s, President Dwight D. Eisenhower added the words “Under God” to the Pledge of Allegiance, doubling down on the Christian values of an anti-communist America. The phrase “In God We Trust” was also added to US currency. As evangelical Christians grew into a crucial voting bloc for the Republican party, communist accusations against the left have appeared now and again to mobilize the base.

Hosted by Kahlil Greene, this video is part of our new series Kahlil Explains that unites Vox’s unique brand of explainer journalism with Greene’s expertise in how politics and culture shape society. This episode traces the history of communism in America and its clash with religious groups to unpack why Democratic candidates are being labeled communists and whether the strategy will resonate with voters today.

Read more about communism and religion in America:

Andrew Hartman’s book Karl Marx in America: https://press.uchicago.edu/ucp/books/book/chicago/K/bo245100866.html

items.title: Grokking the Brain: What AI Reveals About How You Learn • Barbara Oakley • GOTO Copenhagen 2026
items.author: GOTO Conferences
items.content:
<article>This presentation was recorded at GOTO Copenhagen 2026. #GOTOcon #GOTOcph
Join us at GOTO Copenhagen 2027, October 4–8. https://gotocph.com/2027?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=video&utm_campaign=cph26-talks

Barbara Oakley - Professor of Engineering at Oakland University @BarbaraOakley 


RESOURCES
https://x.com/Barbara97881398
https://www.linkedin.com/in/barbaraoakley/
https://barbaraoakley.com/
https://gotopia.tech/experts/1554/barbara-oakley


ABSTRACT
Train an AI model long past the point where it has memorized its examples, and something strange happens — it stops memorizing and suddenly "groks" the pattern beneath them. That hard-won pattern can then be "distilled" into a smaller, faster model that runs it with ease. These are ideas from AI — but they may give us our clearest view yet of the human brain. We grok a hard skill slowly, with conscious effort, then distill it into a fast, automatic system that needs no effort at all. That is what expertise is.

The same “machinery” has a quieter side. A model is aligned by its training data — and in an analogous fashion, so are humans. Give me a child to the age of seven, the old saying goes, and I'll show you the adult. But adults are aligned too, usually without knowing it — and a brain aligned a little too well can harden into a mental fortress, deflecting new ideas.

Curiosity provides a way out. Dopamine—reward-based learning—fuels the brain's ability to rewire — it helps us build new links, keeps the fortress gate open, and keeps hard-won knowledge from setting into a wall. We'll look at what all this means for how you learn, how you use AI, and how you keep thinking for yourself in an age that makes it easy not to.

ABSTRACT
Oh great, another session about AI. Your social media feeds are already flooded with agentic this and spec-driven that; one-shot rewrites and everyone-is-a-programmer-now.

I am not using genAI to go faster but to go broader. It lets me offload (significant) side concerns in areas where I am competent but have no wish to become proficient; the time-sink supporting work that I would either hack together badly myself or side-step altogether.

I want to share some models and metaphors that are helping me make sense of this new world: why Ward Cunningham hates printers; how riding a fixie isn’t really cycling; why I'm treating Claude as a fantastic researcher and a terrible programmer; how test-first is the new TDD.

I am calling this adjacent engineering. Sometimes these side quests become significant enough to spin off into their own entire product, which I call adjacent discovery.

My goal is to give you a more nuanced take on generative AI, to help you cut through all the noise and get actual work done.

items.title: Inside the Deadly 1993 Firefight in Somalia | Ambush in Mogadishu (full documentary) | FRONTLINE
items.author: FRONTLINE PBS | Official
items.content:
<article>The inside story of a tragic 1993 battle in Mogadishu, Somalia, that left 18 Americans and hundreds of Somalis dead. At the time, it was known as the most violent U.S. combat firefight since Vietnam. The battle of Mogadishu went on to inspire the movie “Black Hawk Down.” (Aired 1998)

This journalism is made possible by viewers like you. Donate to FRONTLINE now: https://bit.ly/47DFzCb

And support your local PBS station here: https://www.pbs.org/donate
On Oct. 3, 1993, a planned 90-minute U.S. mission to capture Somali warlord Mohammed Farah Aidid in Mogadishu turned into a deadly 17-hour urban firefight in which hundreds of people died. Armed with automatic weapons and rocket-propelled grenades, Somali fighters shot down two U.S. military helicopters and ambushed elite U.S. Army Rangers and Delta Force units. The Clinton administration would announce plans to withdraw U.S. forces from Somalia days later.

The 1998 documentary “Ambush in Mogadishu” investigates what led up to the disaster — including a civil war and famine in Somalia, attacks on U.N. peacekeepers by Aidid’s forces, muddled U.S. military and diplomatic policy on Somalia, and Washington, D.C.’s failure to coordinate with the U.S. military on the ground.

In forensic detail, “Ambush in Mogadishu” goes inside the firefight that trapped a number of U.S. Army Rangers as they moved into a maze of alleys in Mogadishu to try to save comrades on a downed Black Hawk helicopter. In the documentary, surviving Rangers paint extraordinarily vivid pictures of an intense and bloody battle that took a deadly toll on U.S. forces and also killed an estimated 350-1,000 Somalis, including civilians.

The battle of Mogadishu went on to cast a long shadow on U.S. military decision-making about humanitarian and peacekeeping operations. Part of the tragedy’s legacy, experts said in the documentary, was a U.S. reluctance to be drawn into crises in the ‘90s in other volatile countries, such as Bosnia, Rwanda and Haiti.

ABSTRACT
Have you seen early productivity gains from AI, only to watch them disappear under growing complexity and production incidents? You're not alone. There's a common reason: many production systems already struggle with technical debt. When AI agents enter the development loop, that debt becomes a multiplier. Poor-quality code not only increases defects and costs. It dramatically raises AI risk by driving high breakage rates, turning promising AI agents into legacy code generators rather than genuine help.

Fortunately, there's hope on the horizon. In this talk, Adam Tornhill shows how organizations can achieve both speed and quality with AI. Backed by large-scale empirical studies on AI coding and developer productivity, we separate what works from what doesn't in real-world systems. Building on these findings, we then look at a practical framework for driving and sustaining AI-friendly code at scale. The AI revolution is here. Is your code ready?

items.title: Decoding conflicts - Sudan: The forgotten war | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>Tens of thousands have died in Sudan's war, and millions have been displaced. Why is the world's largest humanitarian crisis receiving so little attention?

War has raged in Sudan since April 2023, when the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces began fighting the Sudanese army. Civilians have paid the price for this power struggle. The situation in Darfur is particularly dire, where experts and the United Nations have long warned of signs of genocide.

Why is this war receiving so little international attention? What impact will cuts to international aid have on a country facing such an immense humanitarian crisis? And what role are outside powers such as the United Arab Emirates, Egypt, Russia and the United States playing in the conflict? What interests drive these governments to support one side or the other with weapons and funding?

Accounts from those affected reveal the devastating impact of the war on the people of Sudan. A journalist from El Fasher, forced to flee the city, discovers videos of murdered family members and friends circulating on social media. A young doctor spent years performing surgery in trenches or amid bombardment. Experts had warned of a looming humanitarian catastrophe for years. Yet the crisis has continued to escalate. Meanwhile, young Sudanese people are fighting to draw the world's attention to what is happening in their country. This film traces the origins of the conflict, who is fueling it, and what responsibility Europe shares.

Ethiopia was spending billions of dollars every year on imported fuel it couldn’t afford, and subsequently defaulted on its debt. Cheap hydropower from Africa’s largest dam made electric vehicles a practical alternative, and Chinese-made EVs — some assembled locally — quickly filled dealership lots. Today, Ethiopia’s EV share outpaces the global average. But sticker prices are too high for most, the grid remains patchy and armed conflict is flaring in the country and across the region. Can Ethiopia make its unprecedented bet on EVs pay off?

Sophia Drossopoulou - Professor at Imperial College London & 2023 Dahl-Nygaard Prize Winner

ORIGINAL TALK TITLE
Specification and Verification of Robust Open Systems: Capabilities, Effects, and Trusted Mediation

RESOURCES
https://www.linkedin.com/in/sophiadrossopoulou

ABSTRACT
Today's complex software is open: trusted internal code is tightly intertwined with untrusted external code whose behaviour may be unknown, or even adversarial. Writing robust internal code in such settings is challenging — programmers must account for the potential effects of calls to external code even when that code cannot be inspected or trusted. These effects can be limited if internal code is written defensively, restricting the effects of external calls by ensuring that these effects can only be caused through access to certain capabilities. items.title: No future in Germany? Why skilled Polish workers are going home | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>Ever more Poles are leaving Germany, while fewer and fewer are moving the other way. Why do they no longer see a future for themselves in Germany? What's drawing them back to Poland? And what does it all mean for German companies?

Philip Panek chose his university with a goal in mind: the European University Viadrina in Frankfurt on the Oder, right on the German-Polish border. When he began his studies, he planned to stay in Germany and build a career there. Now, he's planning to complete his legal traineeship in Poland. There, he says, he has more than just family and friends waiting for him — he also sees new economic opportunities.

Michael Sünkler can also see that Germany is losing its appeal for many Polish workers. The managing director of a transportation company has many employees from Poland. In recent years, however, many have left. For him, the departure of skilled Polish workers is not an abstract political issue — it's a tangible economic problem. One of those employees is Tomasz. The truck driver has worked in Berlin for over ten years, but rising living costs are taking their toll. Rent and groceries have become significantly more expensive, he says. As soon as his daughter finishes school, he plans to return to Poland with his family.

Kamila Gierko and her husband, Zbyszek Perzyna, have already done just that. Six months ago, they moved from Berlin to Szczecin. For years, Germany offered them favorable conditions for self-employment. But bureaucracy and a lack of digital services, along with high taxes and social contributions were increasingly weighing them down. Their experiences in Poland have been very different: More administrative processes are digital, and the tax burden is lower. Germany, they say, has lost its momentum.

This report follows people whose real-life decisions reveal more than statistics can. It profiles a law student who wants to start a career and a family in Poland, an entrepreneur fighting to retain every Polish employee he can, a truck driver reassessing the cost-benefit analysis of his life, and a couple who have already moved back to their home country.



#documentary #dwdocumentary #dwdocs

items.content:
<article>From the unbelievable story of Phineas Gage, whose personality changed after a horrific brain injury, to the enigmatic Gloria Ramirez, the so-called “Toxic Woman” who reportedly caused medical staff to become mysteriously ill, history is filled with medical mysteries so bizarre they continue to baffle doctors and scientists.
